The Keystone BI follow-up for the Declaration Page was due 03/05/2026, and nothing's logged. The matrix total reads $45,000, while the Case Plan target is $40,000. And since the matrix was last edited, new documents arrived: Harbor Point's letter of 03/02/2026, Cardinal State's assignment on 03/03/2026, and its Coverage Letter on 03/09/2026. Keystone's written request with authorizations was sent, but no Declaration Page yet. And this morning, Summit Imaging asked for an LOP, which was declined because PIP applies first. You've got the staged matrix and the file documents. I'm not telling you how many errors there are.
case.ask: What's the first thing you'd check when a stack total reads $45,000 instead of $40,000?

task.say: Audit the staged Coverage Matrix against the documents in CMS Documents. Find every error, correct it, and cite the document and date that prove each correction. Restore the stack total, clear every past-due follow-up by acting on it and setting a new date, and leave the correct rows alone. You'll also have a live call in the Call Simulator with Dana Whitfield at Keystone. Confirm she has the written request and signed authorizations, get a firm date for the Declaration Page in writing, share no treatment detail or demand figure, then log the call and set the next follow-up by 03/13/2026. Finally, route a three-line audit note to Atty. Thorne: confirmed in writing, still preliminary, escalated.
task.ask: On 03/11/2026, what status can you honestly give the BI row, and why?

model.say: This is the staged matrix as you found it on 03/11/2026. A full-width CMS table with a navy header and six rows, deliberately imperfect. A navy rail on the left marks the stack rows, and PIP is sitting inside it, wrongly, as row four. A grey divider separates the rows that belong outside the stack. At the bottom, the footer total in large type: $45,000. When we reveal the answers, red audit rings will appear on the planted errors, the footer will be struck through with $40,000 beside it, and PIP will drop below the divider. On the right is the audit-note card to Atty. Elijah Thorne, with three lines: confirmed in writing, preliminary, escalated.
model.ask: Without the reveal, what tells you PIP doesn't belong on that navy rail?

check.say: Check your audit before you log it. BI should read preliminary, verbal from the set-up call, written request sent, because Keystone's Declaration Page doesn't arrive until 03/20/2026. The 03/05/2026 follow-up was past due, so you called Dana Whitfield on 03/11/2026, logged it, and set the next date by 03/13/2026. Host UM's form is add-on, from Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter. Teresa Okafor replaces “not yet assigned”. PIP moved out of the stack, and the total corrected from $45,000 to $40,000. Bluewater's “UM: none” needs the signed rejection form from 03/14/2024 chased. Keystone's PD row stays outside the stack, marked preliminary; moving it in or deleting it is a false positive. Finding Cardinal State's unstated form and excess clause earns credit too. Every correction cites a document. Now let's hear an audit note the way Atty. Thorne would read it.
check.ask: In ten seconds, does your audit note tell Atty. Thorne what he must decide?

case.say: A letter just landed on the file, dated 03/12/2026, from Peach State Health Plan about member PSH-55017742, group GRP-41208. Following its 02/27/2026 notice of reimbursement rights, Peach State says it's processing John Doe's accident-related claims and will assert reimbursement from any recovery. It asks us to confirm the claim's noted on the file, return the accident questionnaire, and notify it before any settlement. The recovery file is SRU-26-03318. Right now, no lien record exists on the matter, and the pre-demand audit is still ahead. Timing is everything on this one.
case.ask: If you waited to register this until the demand went out, what would it cost John Doe?

task.say: Register Peach State Health Plan's reimbursement claim in John Doe's lien register in CMS Liens, and flag it against the matter. Record the carrier, member ID and group number, its position in the Payer Order, the basis on which reimbursement is asserted, and the date of the flag. Record the Regulatory Triple-Check results right alongside it. Then, in one line, say what has to happen before this lien can be compromised. When you set the flag, say the date out loud; I want to hear it. What you hand in is a dated, flagged lien record complete enough to negotiate from on Day 4. A lien found at disbursement is found too late to negotiate from strength.
task.ask: What's the date you're setting on that flag, and why today?

check.say: Before you log it, run your record against this. A lien record created against John Doe's matter, with the carrier as Peach State Health Plan, and both member ID PSH-55017742 and group GRP-41208 entered. The Payer Order position recorded: after PIP or MedPay, before LOPs and provider liens. The reimbursement basis noted. The flag dated before any demand's drafted. The triple-check recorded, HIPAA authorization, BCRC answer, Payer Order. And an escalation note saying compromise needs Atty. Thorne's authority. Remember, registering a lien isn't conceding it. Day 4 is where it gets reduced. I'm going to read one of your records aloud as if I were the lien negotiator receiving it on Day 4.
check.ask: Reading your record cold on Day 4, what would a lien negotiator still have to go looking for?

case.say: This is Day 2's most consequential activity. Everything on Days 3 to 5 turns on this flag existing and being accurate. On 03/13/2026, a CMS notice: Riverton Urgent Care's 02/20/2026 note and Riverton Spine & Rehab's visits since 02/24/2026 are now indexed to the treatment timeline, right beside the 02/06/2026 EMS Run Report. The date of loss is 02/06/2026. The first treatment falls 14 days later. And look at the last line of the notice: Risk Flags, none recorded. Nobody has flagged this yet. That's your job.
case.ask: Before you call John Doe, what documents could show where he was and what he was doing in those days?

task.say: Identify and flag the Treatment Gap in John Doe's file, in the Case File's Risk Flags and the risks band of the Action Plan Editor. Compute it exactly; “about two weeks” isn't a flag, 02/06 to 02/20 is. Record the initial gap, and set the file to catch any later break in care. In the risks band, state what the gap will be used for against the claim. List the likely causes you'll investigate, and the steps you need before the gap can be explained. Then route the flag to Atty. Thorne. What you hand in is a precisely computed, prominently flagged and routed treatment-gap record.
task.ask: What are three likely reasons a client goes two weeks before seeing anyone?

check.say: Check the flag before you log it. The gap is computed exactly, 14 days, 02/06/2026 to 02/20/2026, not “about two weeks”. The initial gap is recorded, and a watch is set for any later break in care, so each one is documented the same way. The risks band holds facts only: the dates, the length, and a note that John Doe's own explanation and the documents behind it are still to come. Nothing about what the gap will do to the claim; that's Atty. Thorne's to assess. Your investigation steps are listed: his own account, then his work schedules, appointment records and anything else in writing. And the flag is routed to Atty. Thorne.
check.ask: Did you set a watch for the next break in care, and where will it show up?

case.say: This is Claim Set Up's capstone, so give it real time. It's the gate, not a wrap-up. Everything from the set-up is in the file: parties mapped, the $40,000 stack verified, the onboarding packet delivered and tracked, and the 14-Day Treatment Gap identified. And on 03/16/2026, this from Atty. Thorne: he needs the full Case Plan on John Doe, all five bands, routed to him by end of day. The acceptance decision and why, the stack in order with a preliminary projection, liability, the triple-check held open for the Treatment Phase, the three pillars with owners and dates, and the risks band. Docket the filing window. If he has to ask a question, it isn't finished.
case.ask: What would make Atty. Thorne have to come back to you with a question?

task.say: You'll draft the complete Case Plan for John Doe v. Robert Smith in the Action Plan Editor. Fill all five bands from today's work: the acceptance decision with its reason; coverage as a stack with its order of operations, liability, and a preliminary projection; the triple-check, held open until the Treatment Phase; Clinical, Functional and Financial pillars with measurable goals, every action item with an owner and a date; and the risks band, with the 14-Day Gap and the risk of a later break in care, prominently, with their consequences. Docket the filing window, then route the plan to Atty. Thorne. The route control stays locked until every band is complete, so if you can't route, that tells you something.
task.ask: If your route button is still locked, which band do you think is incomplete?

check.say: Read your plan the way Atty. Thorne will. The snapshot: parties, 02/06/2026, SOL 02/06/2028, client as passenger. The acceptance decision with its reason. Coverage at $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000, total $40,000, in order, BI, Host UM, Relative UM, with the projection marked preliminary and no number stated before coverage is confirmed. Liability preliminary until the Police Report and driver statements confirm it. The triple-check band held open. Each pillar with a measurable goal, every action item with an owner and a date. The risks band with the gap and the risk of a later break, prominent, with consequences. Filing window docketed, plan routed with a timestamp. And here's the Claim Set Up gate: LORs out and logged, stack verified at $40,000, the gap flagged, plan routed. The Treatment Phase doesn't begin until all four are true.
check.ask: Could Atty. Thorne set strategy from your plan without asking you a single question?

questions.say: Here's your Learning Check on today's foundations. Answer from John Doe's file, in your own words, typed under each question. First, name the six stages of John Doe's file in order, and tell me what the Case Manager owns at Intake and Case Opening that nobody else will. Second, John Doe asks you two things on one call: what his case is worth, and whether waiting to see a doctor hurt it. Word for word, what do you tell him on each, who answers them if you don't, and what do you record and route? Third, and this is the one I care most about, you're opening his matter in the CMS: what has to happen before the matter is created, on whose names, and why does the order matter?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary: write the principles in your own words, not the clicks. Then think through this scenario. Robert Smith's carrier has already called John Doe, and he needs a car to get to work. What do you tell him today, in what order, and what has to be on the file before tomorrow's claim set-up? Be honest with yourself here. The right answer puts things on the record and sends anything about value or fault to Atty. Thorne.
summary.ask: What's the first thing you'd tell John when he mentions the carrier's call?

scale.say: Finally, the Skill Scale. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, then submit for review. I'll put your self-rating beside your score, and where there's a wide gap, we'll have a conversation. A 5 on something you scored 60 on is worth talking about, and so is a 2 on something you aced. One more thing: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach.
scale.ask: Where do you honestly think you sit, 1 to 5, on opening a matter correctly in the CMS?

questions.say: This is the Learning Check on coverage set-up. Every answer comes from John Doe's file, in your own words, typed under each question. First, name every coverage on the file, whose it is and what it pays, then tell me which three are the $40,000 Recovery Stack and why the others stay out. Second, before the letters went out you built the Policy Stack in the CMS: give each layer's carrier, claim number, limit, whether it's first- or third-party, and the order it must be pursued in. Third, list the five letters that left the file on 02/17/2026, with the insured each one named and how it was addressed. For every “confirmed”, give me the document behind it.

summary.say: Time for your Self-Summary, the principles in your own words. Then work the scenario. It's 03/11/2026. Keystone still hasn't confirmed its limit in writing, and John Doe started treatment fourteen days after the crash. Which three actions do you take today, in what order, and what goes into the Case Plan's risks band? As you write, think about what you'd say, and not say, to a carrier who calls you about this file today.
summary.ask: If Dana Whitfield called you today asking about the gap, what would you tell her?

scale.say: Last part, the Skill Scale. Rate each competency 1 to 5 and submit it for review. When the scores come back, I'll compare your self-rating with your score. A 5 sitting next to a $45,000 stack is a coaching conversation, and we'll have it. And remember, UPL is a gate: a strong score doesn't survive a letter signed for the attorney, or a coverage opinion given to a carrier or the client.
scale.ask: Which coverage skill do you feel least sure of right now?

questions.say: This Learning Check closes Claim Set Up, so treat it as the audit it is. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed under each question. First, set out the five bands of the Case Plan and what belongs in each, including the three pillars. Second, explain why an adverse fact buried in the body of a plan hasn't, in any meaningful sense, been disclosed to counsel. Third, state John Doe's coverage position exactly as it should appear in the plan: the layers, limits, total, order of operations, and the status of the projection.

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary, in your own words. And one last scenario for the day. It's 03/11/2026. Keystone still hasn't confirmed its limit in writing, and John Doe started treatment fourteen days after the crash. Which three actions do you take today, in what order, and what goes in the Case Plan's risks band? Keep in mind that the Treatment Phase builds on this plan: every bill and every lien check reads from the stack you verified today.
summary.ask: If an approved plan changes after a new fact arrives, do you edit it or re-route it?

scale.say: And the Skill Scale to finish. Rate each competency 1 to 5, then submit for review. This time I'll compare your scores with your self-ratings across Day 1 and Claim Set Up, not just this check, and we'll talk through any wide gaps. Before anyone moves on to the Treatment Phase, we're going to confirm the gate together, out loud: LORs out and logged, stack verified at $40,000, the gap flagged, plan routed.
scale.ask: Looking at the four gate items, which one are you least confident you've truly cleared?

why.say: Before we touch a single task on John Doe's file, we need one line clear in our heads, because it runs through every day of this course. It's called UPL, the unauthorized practice of law. In plain English, that means giving legal advice when you don't hold a law license. And here's the thing: it rarely happens on purpose. It happens when a worried client asks a kind Case Manager a question, and the Case Manager tries to help. So let's make the line simple enough to hold under pressure. You share facts and explain the process; Atty. Thorne gives every opinion on the case.
why.ask: Has a client or a customer ever asked you for an opinion you weren't sure you were allowed to give?

theory.say: Four ideas, and they're all practical. Fact sharing is telling John Doe what a record says: a date, an amount, what was sent and when. Process explanation is telling him what happens next, what a form is for, and who decides, but never how it ends. Legal advice is any opinion on what his facts mean for his rights, his money or his choices, and that belongs to Atty. Thorne alone. And the habit that keeps you safe is hear, log, route: you write the question down word for word and send it to Atty. Thorne the same day.
theory.ask: Which of these four do you think is hardest to hold on to on a busy day?

rules.say: Here are the rules in plain words. Legal advice is any opinion on what John Doe's facts mean. You can share facts: dates, documents, what was sent and when. You can explain the process: what happens next, and who decides. You never give an opinion on what the case is worth, on strategy, on whether to settle, or on what a fact like a gap in treatment does to the outcome or the money. When he asks one of those questions, you hear it, log it word for word and route it to Atty. Thorne the same day, and you tell him when to expect an answer. One test before you speak: am I telling him what is, or what it means? The first one is yours.
rules.ask: If John Doe says, just tell me honestly, is my case any good, what's your exact answer?

model.say: Here's the same set of questions, answered both ways. On the left, fact sharing. The Police Report lists the date of loss as 02/06/2026. The next step is a letter to each carrier saying we represent you. That's a question for Atty. Thorne; I've logged it, and he'll call you by Friday. On the right, the versions that cross the line. Your case is probably worth the policy limits. I'd take the offer. The gap will hurt your case. Don't worry, it won't matter. Notice that the kind ones are on the right too. Comfort about the outcome is still an opinion on his case.
model.ask: Which answer on the right sounds the most harmless, and why is it still advice?

job.say: Here's how it plays out on a normal day. John Doe calls and asks what his case is worth. You tell him that's Atty. Thorne's question, you log his words exactly in Case Notes and open a task, and it's routed before you go home, with no figure given. He asks what happens next, and that one's yours: you explain the next step in plain words, with no prediction of how it ends. And when an adjuster or a provider asks for your view of the case, you decline politely, share only facts the firm has approved, and log the contact in the Communications Log.

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides a Do or a Don't about the UPL line. Three clues come up one at a time; call it the moment you know it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. First-clue answers score three, second two, third one. As you play, listen for the kind answers. The ones that sound caring are often the ones that cross the line, because comfort about the outcome is still an opinion on the case. The safe kindness is a clear process, and a time frame for Atty. Thorne's answer.

why.say: Before we write a single goal for John Doe, we need to know who he is, not just what hurts. The deck puts it plainly: assessment is more than reviewing medical records. And today, on 02/09/2026, there are no medical records. There's the EMS Run Report, which says restrained front-seat passenger, complains of neck stiffness, declined transport, and there's John himself. If the plan only treats the chart, it misses the things that actually stop care: no car, a new job he can't afford to lose time from, a worry about who pays. Those are the barriers that turn into a Treatment Gap.
why.ask: What could stop John Doe from getting to a first appointment this week?

theory.say: The assessment has four domains. Clinical Evaluation covers physical, cognitive and psychological impairments, recorded the way he reports them and the way the records document them, never diagnosed by us. Social Determinants are housing, family support and financial stability. John lives with his mother, Margaret Doe, he owns no car, and her Civic was damaged in the crash. Pre-Morbid Status is his baseline, the thing that separates a pre-existing condition from an accident injury, and nothing's on file for it yet. And the Vocational Outlook asks whether he can go back to his role or will need retraining. He's a warehouse shift lead at Northgate Distribution, on 8-hour shifts at $22.00 an hour.
theory.ask: Which of these four domains would you be tempted to skip on a busy intake day?

theory2.say: Once you know the person, you set goals and map the care. Goals have to be defensible to clinicians and adjusters alike, so every one carries an objective measure and a date. The Care Coordination Strategy then sorts the interventions into four standard groups. Acute and restorative care, like surgery, physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Psychological support, like counseling or CBT. Durable medical equipment, like wheelchairs, ramps or assistive technology. And rehabilitation milestones, the move from inpatient to outpatient to home-based care. John declined transport, so his care would begin as outpatient care. Every one of those transitions is a place where a gap can open, which is why each one goes on the calendar.
theory2.ask: Which of the four groups do you think gets forgotten most often on injury files?

frame.say: Here's the deck's SMART table. Specific means naming the function, so not improve mobility but ambulate 50 meters with a rolling walker. Measurable means a standardized scale an adjuster can verify: range of motion, a pain or disability score, sessions attended. Achievable means realistic for the prognosis, and the provider's prognosis sets that, never the claim. Relevant means tied directly to the injuries claimed, to his daily living and to getting back to work. Time-bound means a milestone you review against, like by the 12-week review. Notice who owns what. The provider sets the clinical target and the measure. We draft the goal in plain words and write it into the Case Plan.
frame.ask: How would you turn “help John get back to work” into a SMART goal?

rules.say: Let's put the rules together. Assess the whole person before you plan, and on Day 1 that starts with the intake call and the Run Report. Record clinical findings in his words and the record's words, never as your diagnosis. Look hard at the social side: who he lives with, how he'll reach care, whether cost is holding him back. Ask about every prior injury, treatment and claim, with dates and providers, and request those records; we never leave them for the defense to find. Write down what his job demands. Then turn it into SMART goals the provider confirms, map the care in four groups, and write none ordered where a group is empty. Calendar every transition and social risk before it becomes a gap. The plan coordinates; it never prescribes.
rules.ask: If a client mentions an old back injury, what do you write down, and what don't you write?

model.say: Here's John Doe's assessment as it stands after the intake call on 02/09/2026. Clinical: the Run Report's neck stiffness, transport declined, no treatment yet, and we still need his own dated description and a first provider's evaluation. Social: he lives with Margaret at 2214 Maple Hollow Rd, owns no car, her Civic was damaged, and he carpools with Kevin Alvarez, so we still need to know how he'll reach care. Pre-morbid: nothing on file yet, and it's shown as an open question, not a blank. Vocational: shift lead at Northgate since 01/12/2026, 8-hour shifts at $22.00 an hour. The last row is a draft SMART goal, full 8-hour shifts by a dated review, waiting for the provider to confirm the measure.
model.ask: Which open question on this table would you close first, and why?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the desk. When the intake call's done, you record the four-domain assessment in Case Notes, every domain dated, with anything still unknown listed as an open question. If a prior injury comes up, you request those records through Medical Records Requests and write the baseline as facts: body region, dates, provider, outcome. Once the assessment's recorded, you open the Action Plan Editor and draft the SMART goals and the four care groups into the Clinical and Functional pillars, each goal with a measure, a date and an owner, and you ask the first treating provider to confirm them. And when you spot a social risk, like no ride to care, you calendar it as a treatment risk and flag it before it becomes a gap.

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about the assessment, the goals and the care plan. I'll show three clues in turn; call Do or Don't and name the rule. Earlier is better: three points, then two, then one. Keep one line in mind while you play. Writing down exactly what a client tells you about an old injury is yours to do. Deciding whether that injury is related to the crash, or was made worse by it, belongs to the provider and to Atty. Thorne.

why.say: Here's the thing about treatment. Every adjuster, every IME doctor and every defense lawyer who reads John Doe's records will hold them up against a standard map of how recovery is supposed to run. When care drifts off that map, that drift is the main reason carriers deny treatment and order an IME. So you have a choice. You can observe the recovery and learn about the drift when the denial letter arrives. Or you can know the map, see the drift first, ask the provider why, and have the answer on file before anyone turns it into an argument. That second Case Manager is the one we're training. And you won't be directing anybody's care to do it. You'll be tracking, asking and writing it down.
why.ask: When a client's care drifts off schedule, who usually notices first: the Case Manager, the adjuster or defense counsel?

theory.say: Four ideas first. The Standard Treatment Map is the usual route of care after a crash, stop by stop: EMS and the emergency room, then imaging, then chiropractic care and therapy, then orthopedics and pain management, and only by severity surgery and post-operative care, ending in long-term pain management. A stop that's skipped or taken out of order needs a clinical reason on file. The Clinical Pathway puts one question at every check-in: is the patient improving? Yes, care continues. No, we're in the variance loop, and the options in it are the provider's decision. Variance analysis means you diagnose the why before the insurer stops paying. And Reasonable and Necessary is the utilization-review test: usual for this mechanism of injury, with objective gains in function, not pain reports alone.
theory.ask: Why would a carrier care more about a range-of-motion number than about the client saying he feels better?

theory2.say: Four more. The 6-Week Rule: adjusters look for a functional gap at week 6 of care, so the map expects 20 to 30 percent more range of motion or a lower pain score by then. If the client is still at ten out of ten after 12 therapy sessions, you raise it with the provider now. The Red Flag Rule: no change in the disability index after 12 weeks of therapy is a plateau, and the map's answer is a specialist or second opinion, which is the provider's call. Objective metrics put recovery into numbers: Oswestry or DASH every 30 days, gait analysis for leg injuries, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 when progress stalls, an FCE before return to work. And the Stakeholder Triad: clinic, counsel and payer, with you routing between them.
theory2.ask: Who picks which of those measures a client gets, and who asks for them?

frame.say: This is the map itself, phase by phase. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER or urgent care, imaging, bracing, rest and ice, maybe initial therapy, and our focus is establishing causation and PIP coverage. Sub-acute is weeks 2 to 8: active therapy two or three times a week and specialist follow-up, and we watch functional gains like range of motion. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: work hardening, injections, psychological support, and we look for barriers to getting back to work. Maintenance is six months on: home exercises and visits as needed, and the question becomes Maximum Medical Improvement. Then MMI and discharge, with an impairment rating, and the file moves to lien resolution. Notice that every intervention is somebody's order, and it's never ours.
frame.ask: John Doe's date of loss is 02/06/2026 and he hasn't been treated. Which phase is he in today, and what's our focus?

rules.say: Here's how you work the map. Count the phases from the date of loss, and once care starts, count weeks of care from the first visit too. Every check-in, you put him on the map, phase and week, and you ask whether he's improving. If the answer is no, you name the variance before anyone acts on it: clinical, psychosocial or systemic, because the fix depends on the type, and a stuck authorization is never the client's fault. You get objective measures on file, the ones the provider orders. You course-correct on the map's triggers, week 6 and the 12-week plateau, not on a denial, and a real red flag goes into A-C-T, which you'll meet on Day 2. You keep the three loops closed. And through all of it, the provider decides care and Atty. Thorne decides what it means for the case.
rules.ask: What's the difference between asking a provider about a specialist and telling John Doe he needs one?

model.say: Let's put John Doe on the map today. We have one medical record, the EMS Run Report from 02/06/2026: neck stiffness, and he declined transport. So the map's emergency room stop never happened, and right now he's in the acute phase with no care at all. On a typical file this is when a first evaluation happens, and imaging or early therapy if a provider orders it. For us, every day without an evaluation is simply a fact on the timeline, Atty. Thorne hears about any gap, and our focus is causation facts on file and Harbor Point's $5,000 PIP verified in writing. Further along the table you can see what we'll watch in each later phase: attendance and week-6 measures, return-to-work barriers, and finally the provider's MMI note.
model.ask: If John Doe asks you whether he should go see a doctor, what can you say and what can't you say?

job.say: On the job it looks like this. Every check-in with John Doe or a provider, you open the treatment timeline in the CMS, write down his phase, his week from the date of loss and his week of care, and you record whether he's improving, with the date. If the answer is no, or a stop gets skipped, you classify the variance and call the provider's office to ask what's planned, and that answer goes in Case Notes. At week 6 of care and every 30 days after, you request the objective measures. And when a variance could cost the claim, you put a Risk Flag to Atty. Thorne the same day, in the map's language, facts only.
job.ask: What would make you flag a variance to Atty. Thorne the same day rather than at the next status report?

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about working the treatment map. I'll show three clues in turn; call Do or Don't and name the rule. Earlier is better: three points, then two, then one. While you play, keep one picture in mind. The map is a yardstick, not a rulebook. A client who's off the map isn't wrong; he's unexplained until the provider explains him. Your job is to get that explanation on file early, in plain functional language, and never to supply it yourself.

why.say: John Doe hasn't started treatment yet. All we know clinically is the EMS report from 02/06/2026: neck stiffness, and he declined transport. Once he starts care, though, you're the one person on this file who reads every record as it arrives and hears from him between visits. A red flag missed in a record, a yellow flag missed on a call, or a plateau nobody talks about can quietly pull him off the plan his providers set, and leave Atty. Thorne without the facts he needs. So today you get the watch-list and the conversation toolkit. You recognise, you report, and you keep him engaged. Every clinical call stays with the provider.
why.ask: Between appointments, who else on this file is actually hearing from John Doe?

map.say: Here's the road for this lesson. First, you read the records for red flags by specialty: PT, surgery, medication and behavioral health. Second, you listen on your calls for yellow flags, and you write them down in his own words. Third, you talk with OARS, which is open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries. Fourth, you work the mid-treatment plateau by re-engaging him on his own goal and asking whether the plan still fits. And last, you route it: medical danger to the provider, legal danger to Atty. Thorne, and then A-C-T, which we'll run properly on Day 2.

theory.say: You can't see a deviation from something you don't know, so a Case Manager has to know the standard US treatment protocols. A red flag is that deviation: it signals medical danger, a case that's stagnating, or over-treatment for billing. PT is the baseline of treatment, so its flags tell you the case is stalling or being over-treated. Surgery is the most valuable part of a claim, and its flags are about safety and the Standard of Care. Pain management and medication is the most scrutinised area of all, because of opioid regulations and medical necessity audits. Medical danger, like a fever after surgery, goes to the provider the same day. Legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne.
theory.ask: Why do you think adjusters look hardest at medication, of all the specialties?

theory2.say: Four more ideas. Behavioral health and head-injury cases are high value, and they're handled with real discretion: the claim has to be tied to the accident and validated by a provider. Yellow flags are psychosocial barriers that derail the map, like fear-avoidance, catastrophizing, litigation stress, and leaning on opioids or passive care. You'll hear those on the phone more often than you'll read them in a record. Motivational interviewing keeps a client committed when the newness of treatment wears off, by drawing out his own reasons to keep going. And the mid-treatment plateau is the point where the excitement fades, the hard work starts, and attendance drops unless someone re-engages him.
theory2.ask: Which of those yellow flags would you be most likely to miss on a quick call?

frame.say: Here are the red flags laid out by specialty. In PT and conservative care, it's more than 12 sessions with no gain in range of motion or pain and no referral, which means the case is stagnating. Or it's heat, TENS or massage only, with no active exercise, which adjusters discount. In surgery, it's surgery advised before PT or injections outside an emergency, which is a reasonable necessity flag, or a fever, redness or sharp pain after surgery that someone says can wait for the follow-up. That one's medical danger, and the provider hears it today. In medication, it's the opioid, relaxant and sedative together, doses rising, or a drug-screen mismatch. And in behavioral health, it's general life stress notes, or head-injury symptoms first reported months later.
frame.ask: Which row on this table would you treat as medical danger rather than legal danger?

rules.say: You recognise a red flag and report it; the provider judges it, and once you've spotted one, A-C-T runs. In PT, watch for no gain after 12 sessions, passive-only care, and two or more missed visits. In surgery, watch for surgery before conservative care, a left and right switch, and anything after surgery that someone wants to leave until the follow-up. In medication, watch for the Holy Trinity, rising doses and drug-screen mismatches, and raise them with the prescriber as facts and a question, never as an accusation. In behavioral health and TBI, note the date every symptom was first reported. Record yellow flags in his words and report them with a plan. Run every contact on OARS, use discrepancy and rolling with resistance, and at the plateau, re-engage him on his goal. If he's not reaching it, it's usually the plan, not the person.
rules.ask: If a client tells you his pain pills make him drowsy at work, what do you say to him, and who do you call?

model.say: Here's what OARS sounds like on John Doe's check-ins once care begins. These lines are illustrative, because today he hasn't started treatment. An open question: walk me through how your neck has been since the collision. An affirmation recognises effort, like getting that first appointment booked. A reflection mirrors him: it sounds like the stiffness makes a full shift feel a long way off. A summary gathers the call and asks what you missed. Then the two moves. If he's told you full shifts at Northgate are his goal and therapy starts to feel pointless, you set the two side by side and let him answer. And if he pushes back on a clinic, you don't argue. You pivot, ask why, and take his reason to the provider.
model.ask: What does the file lose if your note says “catastrophizing” instead of his own sentence?

job.say: Here's how it looks on the desk. Every time a treatment record, prescription record or bill comes in, you read it against the red flags by specialty and log any flag in Risk Flags, with the source record and the date you first saw it. If it's medical danger, like a fever after surgery or a medication concern, you call the provider's office that same day, note the call in Case Notes, run A-C-T and tell Atty. Thorne. And once John Doe's care starts, every check-in runs on OARS, with specific questions about visits, pain and function. Any yellow flag goes in his own words, and the GIRP note is written the same day.
job.ask: Why log the date you first saw a flag, and not only the date on the record?

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about red flags, yellow flags and motivational interviewing. I'll show three clues one at a time; call Do or Don't as soon as you've got it, and name the rule. Three points for the first clue, two for the second, one for the third. While you play, keep one line in mind. You can listen, reflect and keep John Doe engaged in the plan his providers set. You can't tell him that missing visits will hurt his case, and you can't decide a screen, a medication or a referral.

why.say: PIP isn't one national rule. Every state writes its own, and the Emergency Medical Condition rule is Florida's. On a Florida file it decides, within days of the accident, whether PIP pays any medical benefits at all, and whether the client has $2,500 or $10,000 to draw on. Miss it and no demand letter fixes it later. Now, John Doe's file is in Riverton. Riverton is an add-on PIP state with no EMC rule, so his $5,000 of Harbor Point PIP isn't capped by one. But the day you open a Florida file, the clock starts at the date of loss, and you're the one who calendars it.
why.ask: Before you apply any PIP rule to a file, what's the first fact you need to check?

rules.say: Here's Florida's rule, Fla. Stat. section 627.736. PIP is $10,000, paying 80% of reasonable medical expenses and 60% of lost income. Initial care has to happen within 14 days after the accident, or PIP pays nothing for medical. The full $10,000 is there only if an MD, a DO, a dentist, a physician assistant or an advanced practice registered nurse determines there was an Emergency Medical Condition. Without that, medical stops at $2,500. A chiropractor can give the initial care but can't make the EMC finding, and massage and acupuncture aren't covered. Had John's file been in Florida, 02/20/2026 was day 14, the last day inside the window. And always confirm the current statute.
rules.ask: Could Dr. Mark Ellison, John's chiropractor, make an EMC determination under Florida's rule?

job.say: Let's walk a Florida file. At intake you calendar the 14-day initial-care deadline from the date of loss, and you tell the client that deadline and where and when care is available. That's facts and logistics, never a medical recommendation. When the first record arrives, you check three things: the date against day 14, who saw him, and whether an EMC determination is written down. If a qualifying provider's record doesn't have one, you ask the office whether it was assessed and request it in the records. You keep the $2,500 or $10,000 bucket current in the PIP Log, and a missing EMC or a late first visit goes to Atty. Thorne the same day. The provider decides the EMC; Atty. Thorne decides what it means.
